title: Hypertext, Markup and How Links Connect the Web
learningObjectives: Define hypertext and explain how links connect one document or resource to another.
Explain markup as a way to label content and describe the structure or role of information.
Describe how HTML combines markup with hyperlinks to create interconnected web documents.
Identify the anchor element and explain how its href attribute specifies a navigation destination.
Distinguish absolute URLs, relative URLs, root-relative URLs and fragment identifiers when writing links.
Explain the difference between a link that navigates to a resource and a button that performs an action.
Use descriptive link text that communicates the destination or purpose without relying on phrases such as click here.
Explain how fragment links navigate to an element identified by an id within the current or another document.
Use target and rel attributes deliberately when opening links in a new browsing context.
Recognize that link destinations can be internal pages, external sites, downloadable resources, email addresses or telephone actions.
Explain how browsers, search engines and assistive technologies interpret hyperlinks and link relationships.
Create and test a small set of meaningful internal and external links while checking URL resolution and accessibility.

understand.concept: Hypertext is text or content that contains links to related resources, allowing a reader to move through connected information rather than reading only one fixed sequence. Markup uses elements and attributes to identify the roles and structure of content. HTML combines both ideas: it describes document structure and provides hyperlinks that connect documents, sections, files and other resources. The anchor element (a) represents a hyperlink when it has an href attribute. The destination is a URL, and the link text should communicate where the link leads or what it does.
understand.whyItMatters: Links are a core part of the Web's navigation model. Correct link semantics help people move through a site, help assistive technologies announce destinations, and help browsers and search systems understand relationships between resources. A link is for navigation; a button is for an action such as submitting a form or changing the current interface.
understand.history: The idea of hypertext predates the Web, while HTML used hyperlinks to connect resources across the early Web. The Web's defining strength is not only that documents can be displayed, but that they can refer to other resources using URLs and links. Keep historical dates and named milestones tied to authoritative historical sources when adding them to a published lesson.
understand.analogy: A hyperlink is like a cross-reference in a book that points you to another chapter or source. Hypertext allows many such references to connect documents into a network.
understand.analogyLimit: A web link is more than a printed reference: it can trigger navigation, load a resource, include a fragment, or invoke a protocol handler. The destination may change or become unavailable, and links are resolved using URL rules rather than page numbers.

explain.narrative: The Web connects resources through URLs. HTML uses the anchor element to create a link: `HTML guide`. The href attribute identifies the destination, while the text between the tags is the link's accessible name in the simplest case. Choose link text that describes the destination. A list of links that all say “click here” is difficult to understand when read out of context. A URL may be absolute, such as `https://developer.example.test/guide`, relative to the current document, such as `../guide/`, or root-relative, such as `/guide/`. A fragment identifier beginning with # can point to an element whose id matches that fragment, for example `href="#examples"`. URL resolution depends on the document's base URL and may be affected by a base element. Use an anchor for navigation to another page, resource or location. Use a button for an action in the current interface. Do not choose an element only because it looks like the design you want; CSS can style semantic links and buttons appropriately. If a link opens a new tab using target="_blank", include rel="noopener" for an explicit opener-isolation policy and consider whether opening a new context is necessary. A link to a downloadable file should make that purpose clear. mailto: and tel: links ask the device to handle an email or telephone action; support depends on the user's environment. A fragment link can improve navigation within a long document. Give the destination a stable, unique id and make the link text describe the section. Test links with keyboard navigation and verify that each destination exists. A page can display a link even when its destination is broken, so check the URL and response as part of your testing.

examples.explanation: The a element creates a hyperlink. Its href attribute identifies the destination. Hypertext connects related documents and resources, while markup describes the role and structure of content.
examples.expectedOutput: The browser displays the meaningful HTML content.

examples.title: Anatomy of a hyperlink
examples.code: Explore the HTML course
examples.explanation: The a element represents a hyperlink. href supplies the destination URL. The class is a styling hook, not the destination. Descriptive link text remains understandable when a screen reader lists links separately.
examples.expectedOutput: A link that navigates to the HTML course resource.

examples.explanation: Each URL form has a different base. The fragment points to an element in the current document. Ensure IDs are unique and that the referenced target exists.
examples.expectedOutput: Each link navigates to its intended resource or section.

examples.title: Navigation and actions use different elements
examples.code: Account settings
examples.explanation: The anchor moves to a resource. The button performs an action in the current interface. Both can be styled to look similar, but their semantics and keyboard behaviour differ.
examples.expectedOutput: The link navigates; the button triggers an application action.

examples.title: Open a new browsing context deliberately
examples.code: Open the external reference in a new tab
examples.explanation: target="_blank" requests a new browsing context. rel="noopener" prevents the opened page from receiving an opener reference. Tell users when a link opens a new tab, and avoid doing so when it is not useful.
examples.expectedOutput: The external reference opens in a new tab or window when the browser permits it.

examples.title: Make resource and download destinations clear
examples.code: Download the course outline (PDF) Email support Call support
examples.explanation: The download attribute can suggest a download for same-origin resources, subject to browser and server behaviour. mailto and tel rely on a suitable handler being available on the device.
examples.expectedOutput: Links clearly describe the file or action they request.

practise.guidedTask: Create a page with an internal page link, an external reference link, a fragment link to a lower section and a download link. Use descriptive link text. Add one button for a page action and explain why it is not an anchor. Test every link with a keyboard and inspect the destination URL.
practise.independentTask: Build a small documentation navigation page with links to three internal sections, one external standards reference and one downloadable resource. Include one new-tab link with an explicit rel policy. Check every destination, unique fragment id, link text and keyboard focus order.
hints: Use a for navigation and button for an action.
The href attribute contains a URL; the link's text should explain the destination.
Relative URLs are resolved against the document's base URL.
A fragment such as #examples refers to an element id in the document.
Use descriptive link text rather than repeating click here.
Opening a new tab is a user-experience decision; use target and rel deliberately.
Check that each link destination exists and can be reached with the keyboard.

questions.prompt: What is HTML primarily responsible for?
questions.explanation: HTML describes document structure and meaning.

questions.prompt: How does a browser use HTML?
options: Parses document structure and builds a DOM
Always treats it only as an image
questions.answer: Parses document structure and builds a DOM
questions.explanation: The DOM represents document nodes and their relationships.

questions.prompt: Which element is the semantic choice for navigation to another page?
questions.explanation: An anchor with href represents a hyperlink to a resource.

questions.answer: An element in the current document whose id is examples
questions.explanation: A fragment identifier can navigate to an element with the matching id.

questions.prompt: Why should link text be descriptive?
options: It makes every link open in a new tab.
It automatically validates the destination server.
questions.answer: It helps users understand the destination, including when links are read out of context.
questions.explanation: Descriptive link text supports usability and accessibility.

questions.prompt: Which control should normally perform an action such as saving the current form?
questions.explanation: A button represents an action; an anchor represents navigation.
